name: Hana Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build the front end of a box-office system for small theatres and music venues, the screens where you pick your seat and pay. There are twenty-five of us, and our clients are places with leaky roofs and volunteers on the door. I like making the seat map work for someone using a screen reader, because that's a real person getting into a show. What wears me out is every venue wanting its own colour of button by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, how are things set up for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Priya, who teaches drama, and I volunteer with our street's tenants' group on Tuesdays. The pay's on the low side for a developer, but there are only three or four tech jobs in this city that aren't in a call centre. I've got maybe two and a half weeks of rent saved, which isn't much of a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Part of me thinks that's already where we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what a lot of us suspected, and that's fine. Online I'd probably share a long post about how the money that went into AI could have funded actual public services. At work I'd say let's get back to fixing the seat map for wheelchair spaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't make me feel safe, because my company's problem was never AI. Our venues are skint, and two of them closed last year, which meant fewer licences sold. If three more close, someone on our team goes, and I don't have much money to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI helper for boring stuff like regular expressions, the way I do now, once or twice a week. I'd start a small savings pot and try to get it to two months' rent by next winter. I'd also go back to the tenants' group about the rent rise on our street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, but with a low hum of worry. The theatres and music venues closing keep me up at night, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine bits of your day would AI still take, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the small layout fixes and the test scripts. I already let it write the first draft of a test, then I check it. That's maybe an hour a day, and if that hour vanished for everyone, management might notice they need one fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if a venue closure hit your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and my gym membership, in that order. Priya and I already cook together on Sundays to save money. After that it's the trip home to see my mum in the spring, and I'd hate that.

say: I'd say the **AI money** could have funded real public services instead.
At work I'd say let's get back to fixing **wheelchair spaces** on the seat map.
think: My company's real problem is **struggling venues**, not AI, and two closed last year.
If more venues close, **someone on our team** goes, and I've little money to fall back on.
do: Keep using the **AI helper** once or twice a week for boring code like regular expressions.
Build a **savings pot** worth two months' rent by next winter.
Push the **tenants' group** to fight the rent rise on our street.
feel: Mostly fine, with a **low hum** of worry about **venues closing**.
S0.quote: The theatres and music venues closing keep me up at night, not the robots.
fieldNote: Her worry is tied to **venue finances**, not to AI, which fits the Plateau picture.
She already uses AI **sparingly** and checks its work, a habit that fits her steady style.
The **tenants' group** shows she turns worry into collective action locally.

steps.text: Keep checking AI-drafted test scripts once or twice a week
Save two months' rent in a separate pot by winter
Organise the tenants' group against the street's rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one feels uncomfortably close to real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared, not pocketed. I'd talk about it at the tenants' group and with the developers' union some friends are setting up. I'd also say, honestly, that I use these tools and they're useful, so it's not about smashing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my team shrinks. We're twenty-five, and I can see us being fifteen in three years if the AI can build venue screens from a description. I'm not the best on our team of developers, so I'd be in the middle of the cut list, and middles get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw the others on the team getting faster with it, I'd use the AI tools every day and learn them properly. I'd make myself the person who knows accessibility rules inside out, because that's checking work that needs a human eye. I'd also join that union, finally, instead of just talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not hopeless. I feel like I'd have some say in what happens to me, as long as I don't sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, who does our support emails, because answering customers is right there on your card. He's great with angry box-office managers on a Saturday night. I don't know what he'd do if the AI answered them instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others first. Isn't that risky in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen people burn weeks on a shiny tool that got dropped a month later. I'd wait a month or two, not a year, and watch what the fast people actually keep using.

say: I'd say the **gains** from AI should be shared with workers, not pocketed.
I'd admit I use these tools and find them **useful**, so it's not about smashing them.
think: I can see our team of twenty-five becoming **fifteen** within three years.
I'm in the **middle** of the team on skill, and middles tend to get cut.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly once colleagues prove which ones stick.
Become the team's go-to person for **accessibility rules**, which need a human check.
Join the **developers' union** friends are setting up, instead of just talking about it.
feel: **Nervous** but not hopeless, as long as she keeps **moving**.
S1.quote: I'm not the best on our team of developers, so I'd be in the middle of the cut list, and middles get cut.
fieldNote: She makes a **clear guess** of her team shrinking from 25 to 15.

Worries for **Kofi** in customer support, showing she sees who is exposed first.

steps.text: Learn the team's main AI coding tools after a month's trial
Study for an accessibility testing certificate in the evenings
Join the new developers' union and attend its meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before my flat's next lease renewal but one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need emergency rules: no mass layoffs without notice and a basic income straight away. I'd be organising, not just posting. I'd tell my friends this is the moment to stick together, because it'll be everyone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job goes almost as soon as it arrives. Building box-office screens is pure thinking work, and if AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, the venues will just buy that. The three-year wait for robots doesn't help me, because I don't touch anything with my hands at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back hard and try to pay off my credit card while I still have a salary. I'd ask the venues I know about stage crew work, rigging lights and setting up chairs, because that's hands-on and might last three years longer. I'd lean on Priya and my mum if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. It's the speed that gets me, because you can't plan anything in two years on two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stage crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I did lighting for a student theatre at university, and I still help out at the community theatre near us. It's lifting and climbing ladders, not screens. If thinking jobs go first, the person who can focus a light by hand might have a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry, which is a lie. My mum cleaned offices for twenty years so I could go to university, and now my degree might be worth less than her mop. That'd be hard to say out loud.

say: I'd demand **emergency rules**, including notice before mass layoffs and a basic income.
I'd tell friends to **stick together**, because this would hit everyone at once.
think: Building box-office screens is **pure thinking work**, so my job would go almost at once.
The **three-year gap** before robots doesn't help, because nothing I do is hands-on.
do: Cut back hard and **pay off** my credit card while I still have a salary.
Ask local venues about **stage crew** work, since rigging lights is hands-on.
Lean on **Priya and Mum** for a room or money if it comes to it.
feel: **Frightened** by the speed, with no way to plan on **two weeks** of savings.
S2.quote: My mum cleaned offices for twenty years so I could go to university, and now my degree might be worth less than her mop.
fieldNote: Her **stage crew** idea uses the robot gap smartly, building on real lighting experience.
The **mum** story shows the class pride and pain under her progressive views.
She expects her job to go **almost at once**, which drives the alarmed mood.

steps.text: Pay off the credit card while the salary still comes in
Ask venue managers for paid stage crew and lighting shifts
Move in with Mum or Priya if the rent can't be paid
Organise developers and venue staff to demand layoff notice rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to do something, if I'm honest with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to get it right: a fund paid by the companies, free retraining, and unions at the table. I'd still be organising, but it'd feel less like a fire alarm. I'd tell people to start planning now instead of panicking in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see my developer job lasting maybe three or four more years, getting thinner each year. I'm thirty-two by the time it really bites. I think the smart move is to have one foot in something hands-on before the robots come in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper stage electrics course at the college in the first year, evenings and weekends. I'd ask the community theatre for paid shifts, even if it's just two a month. I'd keep coding the box-office screens full-time while it lasts and save what the course doesn't eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. Five years feels like a plan is possible, if I'm not lazy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans if the robots arrive on time in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've bought myself three years, maybe a bit more. Theatres are slow and weird, and nobody wants a robot dropping a light on an actor. It's not forever. But three years at thirty-five is a lot better than nothing at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd want to bring along with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, definitely. I'd drag him to the electrics course with me. He's good under pressure, and a Saturday night show is all pressure.

I'd tell people to **start planning now** instead of panicking in 2030.

S3.quote: Theatres are slow and weird, and nobody wants a robot dropping a light on an actor.
fieldNote: She uses the **five years** to build a hands-on second skill before thinking work goes.
Her worry is real, but she feels **some control**, which fits anxious rather than alarmed.
Wants to bring **Kofi** along, showing her collective instinct in everyday terms.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening stage electrics course
Take paid lighting shifts at the community theatre twice a month
Keep coding the box-office screens full-time while the job lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is almost a whole career phase. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time. With ten years of warning, if people get hurt it's a political choice. I'd push our union to win retraining time inside work hours. And I'd tell younger developers to think hard about what they study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine for a good while. I'll probably still be a developer at thirty-two, maybe a different kind. The question is what I'm doing at thirty-seven, and I've got years to work that out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep coding and get properly good with the AI tools as they become standard, since that's what keeps me hired for the next few years. Around year four or five I'd start the stage electrics course. I'd build up three months of savings first, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with something in the back of my mind. It's like knowing your lease ends in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd actually start the course in year four, or keep putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start, because I'd be watching others first, which is my thing. If I see friends doing well after switching, I'll follow. If nobody's switching, I'd probably wait too, which might be a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this picture feel worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the venues start closing anyway, because then my job goes early for a boring reason. That's the part ten years doesn't fix.

I'd push the union to win **retraining time** inside paid work hours.
think: I'd probably still be a developer at **thirty-two**, just a different kind.
The real question is what I'm doing at **thirty-seven**, and I have years to decide.
do: Get properly good with the **AI tools** as they become standard at work.
Start the **stage electrics course** around year four or five.
Build up **three months** of savings slowly before switching anything.
feel: Mostly **okay**, like knowing your **lease ends** in a few years.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, if people get hurt it's a political choice.
fieldNote: With a decade, her own job feels **safe for now**, so the worry sits in the background.
Her **follow-others** habit could make her wait too long, which she half admits.
The **venue closures** stay her nearer risk, which ten years doesn't fix.

steps.text: Learn the AI coding tools as they become standard at work
Start the stage electrics course around year four
Build savings up to three months' rent before switching

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years with two weeks of savings isn't a plan, it's a fall. What would help is a basic income that starts the day the layoffs do, and rent controls so people like me don't lose the flat while we work it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people around us. I'm not scared only for me; I'm scared for Kofi, for my mum, for the volunteers on the theatre door. Nobody in this story gets through it alone.

headlineQuote: Two years with two weeks of savings isn't a plan, it's a fall.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** front-end developer building box-office screens for small theatres.
She shares a flat with her friend Priya and has about two and a half **weeks of rent** saved.
She uses AI **now and then**, waiting to see what others keep before committing.
Her worries start with **closing venues** and grow to alarm when AGI comes in two years.
Her plan is **stage electrics**, a hands-on skill, plus union organising alongside.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two weeks of savings gives her no time to switch.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** that starts the day layoffs do.
**Rent controls** so she keeps her flat while retraining.
